1.t: Learning guitar from Bill Johnson's loaned instrument
1.s: Bill Johnson loaned him a guitar and showed him four basic chords, which Barker mapped onto his ukulele knowledge.
1.q: Luis Russell’s man. Yeah, Bill, that’s who. I can’t think of his last name. He had a guitar, two guitars on a stand when I saw him. So he say, “Go ask him to loan you a guitar.” Your uncle’s in the band. He knows you. You ain’t going to run away with the guitar. So I went to see him, and he loaned…

1.t: Buying his mother's ukulele for 25 cents a week
1.s: His mother sold him the ukulele for half its price, and Ashton Murray tuned it and showed him chords.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: So I said... Well, I saw this ukelele. So I asked Ma, I said, 'What did you do with that ukelele?' She said, 'I'm not doin' nothin' with it.' [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE] I said, 'Why don't you give it to me.' She said, 'I'm not goin' to give it to you.' She said, 'I'll sell it to you.' I said, 'What do…

1.t: Banjo lessons, straight rhythm playing and Narvin Kimball
1.s: Barker took lessons from George Augustin, observes that banjo players mostly played a straight beat, and praises Kimball's showmanship and seriousness.
1.q: Yeah, I’ve taken guitar lessons . . . wouldn’t say it was lessons, from George Augustin, who was supposed to be a good banjo player. I took some lessons from him, every Sunday for about a summer. Got the basics, but I was getting the basics of playing by ear, because none of them, rarely any of…

1.t: Charlie Costain and the song Chinaman and Mabel
1.s: Danny played ukulele with his Creole friend Charlie Costain, who sang honky-tonk songs and later became a wine-drinker at the jukebox.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: Charlie Costain(?), I meet him. He was another little kid. He played a little ukelele. And I go to his house, and he's in there, his mother's hitting him on the wrist(?) because he wasn't playing the piano right. If he was playing the piano right, what ...(? )...(? )... He sang, "Chinaman and…

1.t: Ashton Murray and Herman Henderson, the ukulele kids
1.s: Neighborhood boys Ashton Murray and Herman Henderson played ukulele and impressed him.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: So that was that. So it was just a matter of you picking up music if you wanted to. So a little kid in the neighborhood was playin' the ukelele. His Daddy was a mailman, and he had this ukelele. He could play it -- somewhat. And the ukelele craze had come on, and everybody had ukeleles. My aunt…

248.t: His mother bought him a one-dollar guitar and he taught himself
248.s: Dawson tells how his mother bought an old guitar for a dollar from a player and he learned to tune and play it himself.
248.ch: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
248.q: And that started me to play. You see, I took my mama, bought the guitar for me for one dollar. She said, my son likes music. I think he's going to make good because he's interested in music. So she said, someday I'm going to get him a guitar and let him work out on it. So he said, well, he can have…

248.s: Dawson says he began on guitar, then banjo and mandolin, which he learned by ear while serenading.
248.q: Well, in fact, I'll tell you the truth, I believe I did start on the guitar first, but I, I, I, I, I played, I practically was playing both of them most at the same time, you see, because I could play guitar pretty good. Mm-hmm. And banjos, when they, a long time ago, the banjo came out behind the…

248.t: Guitar lessons and learning from Fess Manetta
248.s: A white visitor gave him four guitar lessons; Manetta helped; he moved to tenor banjo after six or seven years of guitar.
248.q: No, I had a, I had a white, uh, fellow that gave me a few lessons, but he was, uh, with, uh, off from circuit. He came here and he stayed about a month. I take about four lessons from him and he had to go away then. Remember his name? No. He didn't get his name. I remember. He just gave me, he just…

248.t: Dawson's birth date and first instruments
248.s: Dawson gives his birth date (24 July 1884) and says he taught himself, starting at about 18 on tenor banjo and guitar.
248.q: The End The End Okay, I'm going to get the date. 31st of January 1962, Eddie Dawson, Type 1. Can you tell us your birth date, Eddie? When were you born? 19...let me see...24th of July. 24th of July. What year would that be? That was...1884. Uh huh. And did any of your family play instruments before…

44.t: Grandfather's banjo and learning from Papa Charlie Jackson records
44.s: Welch learned on his grandfather's banjo and Papa Charlie Jackson records, teaching himself.
44.q: No, sir. Well, when I first learned how to play, my grandfather had an old five-string banjo. Mm-hmm. And so... When those fellas leave our home, I'd take that old banjo and go in there and start to grab a phone. Oh, you know those grab phones used to wind up? You know, Charlie Jackson record on

44.t: Building a cigar-box guitar; Maxey's first guitar
44.s: Pete began in 1934 on a homemade copper-wire guitar; Maxey recalls starting on a twelve-string.
44.q: Well, I started in the music business in 1934. 1934. 1934. 1934. And when did you start learning? Well, I just picked on up from then. Just start learning. I made my first guitar. Yeah, you made it yourself? I made it myself. That's what I learned on. Yeah. From that on, then I went and bought me…

44.t: Grandfather's songs and learning bottleneck from Frank Banglin
44.s: Welch cannot recall grandfather's songs; Frank Banglin taught him bottleneck guitar.
44.q: know ! boy I used to play with in Deeson Mississippi called Frank Banglin he learned me to play with the bottleneck I saw him play once and I came on back home and got me a co-cola bottleneck cut it off and fixed it up and tried to play and finally learned

44.t: Playing alone with guitar, kazoo and harmonica
44.s: Pete repeats his cigar-box guitar story and says he played by himself with guitar and kazoo.
44.q: I went and bought me old cheap guitar. Oh, the strings was sitting just about an inch from the neck. But I went on with it. Right. Finally, I run across a really good guitar. And that's why I learned really good. And I just picked it up and went on. Music for getting to follow me then.

182.t: Moving from guitar to violin and cornet
182.s: He began guitar around 17, found it too slow, took up violin and later bought a cornet; he played guitar alone at first.
182.q: Yeah, before I took up the violin. Then I take the violin. But the cornet, I didn't take it. I know the music. Yeah. All I had to do, by a method. And, uh, at the, uh, fainting, you understand? Get the tone, A, B, you know, after I got the tone, I know the music, that's all. I just wanted to know…

182.t: Learning guitar and tuning by ear
182.s: Tom picked up guitar without lessons, playing in the streets, and learned tuning by listening to others; he says he has the tone in his head.
182.q: Yeah, I didn't take a lesson. I just would go around and play it in guitar. I don't play in no band, just around the streets you understand? Oh I see. Yes. Then I take the violin, then I start to play it in the band, lead the band. That got too slow and I picked up the connet. I see. I just bought…

182.t: First guitar, violin lessons and learning to count time
182.s: He started on guitar self-taught, then took violin lessons from an old professor, first spending months on counting 'division' with hand and foot.
182.q: Guitar. Guitar, the first instrument. Did you have any lessons on it or just pick it up? No, just picked it up. And violin, I take lessons. You took lessons on that? Yeah, I take lessons from the old professor from the French Opry. Jimmy Fallow, he died. He was taking lessons. And when he takes his…

270.t: Switching to banjo and rehearsing with George Morris, Thomas Mack and Edmund Washington
270.s: Sayles explains how he took over his brother's banjo while his friends, all pupils of Dave Perkins, had trumpet, trombone and clarinet lessons and rehearsed together.
270.ch: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
270.q: we're talking about the mud yeah I was saying about I remember when he played there at this big place at San Su and I remember from leaving that job and when I played that down he left there and went to California mm-hmm you see now what I should have got back at the time when I say on ramp when we…

270.t: Taking up banjo and teaching himself
270.s: He learned banjo while teaching his brother, reading from violin training and piano parts; Perkins taught him only violin.
270.q: No, well, you see, after I'd been playing with this band, I was, my oldest brother was working for a world artist. And he bought a banjo and I was teaching him how to play the banjo. And at the same time, I was learning myself.

270.t: Learning guitar, banjo and violin technique
270.s: He taught himself banjo and guitar after learning to read through violin.
270.q: The one thing about it, I didn't learn to like somebody playing the violin, a teacher, you learn to position the thing out of, you know, to regulate your hands, like you do with any strings. I didn't learn that, but I did learn how it was a pretty good reader on it, you see. I didn't learn how to…

293.t: Getting his first banjo and learning to play
293.s: A fellow gave him a five-string banjo, he taught himself from a book, and soon bought and sold many banjos.
293.ch: Banjo, piano and his own bands
293.q: I had a practice. A fellow by the name of Wallace. Wallace gave me that banjo. A five string banjo. And I started to play it and I bought me a book. And I started to play in it. And the fellow knocked on my door and said, Hey man, I need a banjo player for tonight. I said, I don't play no banjo. He…

293.s: Interviewer confirms the pronunciation and spelling of Bourgeau and the nickname Fan. He says he began playing before 1929, first plectum banjo, then piano.
293.q: I looked like a Chinaman, that's why they call me that. And we started, I started around 29. No, I started before 29 playing with different little bands. And I first started playing with a plectum banjo. Was that five strings? Five strings, plectum banjo. Then I left it go and I began to play piano…

293.t: First instruments and the Orleans Pleasure Club
293.s: Started around nine, learning guitar from Johnnie Simpson, then banjo and piano, practicing on the club piano at the Orleans Pleasure Club where Jelly Roll Morton played on Mondays.
293.q: Well I started to play when I was around. Johnnie Simpson was the one who taught me how to play the guitar. Well he started. When I got away from it, you see what I mean? I was around nine years old.

837.t: Guitar lessons, dancing school trio and Armand's Pass Christian band
837.s: A grandmother, an aunt's ukulele and three failed classical guitar lessons come first. Ragtime players at a neighbour's dancing school then draw him back to the guitar. He takes cheap lessons from the chauffeur-bandleader Armand and hears Buddy Petit's band compete with him.
837.q: My grandmother is actually the one who got me interested in music. She used to play piano a little bit and she'd get songs and knew enough about them. I remember probably the first two that she tried to teach me was one of them. Oh, my baby, my curly-headed baby, we'll sit beneath the sky and sing…

837.t: Going out to parties, meeting his wife, and the rival Invincibles
837.s: After three years of practice, at about fourteen the group begins playing at girls' houses, where he meets his future wife. The better string group, the Invincibles, becomes the Owls.
837.q: Oh, I would say around 11, 12 years old. That's all. Maybe 14 years, I don't know you. Not that old. No, we didn't ever leave that house for three years. We practiced until we were about 14. Then we began going out. Now there were a lot of older men in the crowd, and I wouldn't say older. Oh yeah,…

837.t: The Reynolds brothers' Sunday string group
837.s: At about eleven he joins Bob and Harry Reynolds' Sunday sessions on Britannia Street. He lists the group: violinists Hilton Harrison and Rex, Bernie Shields on banjo, Charlie Hardy on ukulele and Bill Gibbons.
837.q: Then along the line here, I would say around, I must have been no older than 12, maybe 11. We suddenly discovered there were other boys that were playing. We never had gotten together. Everybody was afraid to come out, afraid to show how little they knew. But finally, I went at an invitation to Bob…

848.t: First instruments: piano, violin and a homemade banjo
848.s: He disliked piano and violin, built a stringed instrument from a seagull box, and Coochie Martin's guitar strings; the kitchen trio.
848.q: That's right. And, uh, I didn't like the piano. I didn't like that because at that time, uh, they had things that was called your music role. Oh yeah. It'd fold up. And sometimes it was made out of plush and different colors like that. And they passed down from my sister to me her music role that…

848.s: Buying a ukulele with savings, admiring Red Allen's playing, and linking dates to his father's start on the Capitol.
848.q: Well, I made that, I made that, uh, supposedly ukulele or banjo, whatever it was, and cut a hole in it, and would play with that. And, uh, I was in high school. And, uh, when I was in high school, later on when I went to high school, I, uh, I bought a ukulele. I had a little job in the afternoons…

126.t: Receiving a ukulele from his uncle in 1914
126.s: An uncle brought a ukulele back from Honolulu and gave it to Hardy; nobody knew how to tune it, so friends suggested the top four guitar strings.
126.q: Well, it's a strange thing. My father's brother married and went to Honolulu on his honeymoon. And he saw these little bitty ukuleles and had these boys strumming on and so forth, and he decided to buy one and bring it back with him. He didn't know anything at all about playing music of any kind.…

126.t: Learning by ear and the formation of the 6 and 7/8 band
126.s: No formal lessons; he learned chords from friends and worked hard at it. School friends formed the band before World War I.
126.q: Oh, I really boned on it. I mean, I tried my best to learn all there was to know about it, even in the early days before the First World War. And strangely enough, at that time, there were quite a number of boys that I went to school with that played various musical instruments. And it was in those…

276.t: Starting to serenade, Frank Wagner and learning
276.s: Began serenading in 1922, picked up lessons informally, and played with guitarist Frank Wagner, whose suicide he describes.
276.q: Well, I used to fool around a musician, they taught me a few things. Fester Monette crossed the river. And I used to be with one of the best guitar players in town, they called him Frank Wagner. He hung himself. He was working on the P.W.A., things got rough around there and he couldn't support his…

276.t: First instruments: guitar, mandolin, ukulele, banjo
276.s: Guitar at about 13, then mandolin briefly, then ukulele while selling them at Morris Music Shop; banjo around 1925.
276.q: My first instrument was the guitar was my first instrument. So I quit playing the guitar and started fooling the mandolin. So I stayed on the ukulele. I never did quit the ukulele. I stayed there with the ukulele.

968.t: John Marrero's instruments, his wife, and self-teaching
968.s: John played banjo, guitar and piano, taught himself under their father; his widow could tell more about him.
968.q: Well, tomorrow, remember, that's all John did to play ghetto. That time we had six strings banjo, which he was then. Oh yeah. Yeah, you remember that six strings banjo. Well, he played a lot of piano too.

968.t: Simon on bass, father teaching the sons, first guitar
968.s: Their father taught all the sons; Simon became the bass player; Lawrence's first instrument was a six-string guitar shown by John.
968.q: No, they didn't get them. They all, we all learned on one of the instruments. Uh-huh. See? And I did pick up sousaphone one time, but it was a little difficult for me so I wouldn't bother with it anymore. But the bass, I also did pick up the bass. I used to play bass. Yeah, I was in the first class…

713.t: His first guitar, a cheap one bought by his father
713.s: Nelson's first guitar was a cheap, funny little instrument his father brought him in the country at age eight, and his small hand could only finger half of it.
713.ch: Second reel: instrument, style and wrap-up
713.q: Yeah it was a big guitar. I used to finger, you know, half. Yeah. I didn't have to finger all the way I finger would go, as much as I could.

713.t: Starting guitar at eight; brother Henry 'Stacks' Nelson
713.s: Nelson taught himself a six-string at eight, moved to the city at about ten, and says his older brother Henry Nelson, called Stacks, also played guitar.
713.q: around the here in New Orleans yeah all over because I used to call him stacks everybody stacks I've heard the name yeah is he still living no he did how much older was he than you he was but

284.t: Deciding to buy a guitar at sixteen
284.s: Friends play instruments; a drummer friend steers him to guitar, and he sends away for one but finds no teachers.
284.q: Well, when I was around the age, when I got around 16 years old, I had a, I used to go around with boys, most of my friends, you know, they had a few that played piano. And one boy I remember with a fine violin playing. In other words, he could play most any of the string instruments. Yes. The…

284.t: Teaching himself guitar from the tuning fork and book
284.s: After two years in Chicago he finds the diagram book and tuning fork in the guitar box and tunes it himself; a friend wants to buy it.
284.q: So, I kind of give up on that guitar. I'll just let it stay there. I got it in a big box. You see? And just the way that box come, I set that guitar around in there. I didn't see that guitar in the morning for about two years. I went away. I went to Chicago and I stayed in Chicago about two years.…

194.t: Learning boogie woogie, trying guitar and sticking with piano
194.s: He learned boogie woogie quickly, argues that you can learn music by playing, tried guitar and other instruments around 1934-35, and returned to piano.
194.q: They had electric guitars in there, though. I learned how to chord on the guitar. One key in, I key C, you know. Everything we played, every day and C, because that's all I knew. And the playing started getting calm and getting soul. Went back to the piano, and I just stuck with that, you know. I…

194.t: First real instrument was a cheap guitar
194.s: He answers that his first instrument was an acoustic guitar; he played chords, best in C, but strings kept breaking and he gave it up.
194.q: Well I could play the whole- I could play the whole chord though. I could play four, six, eight. I could play in C very well.

476.t: Banjo tuned like a ukulele; piano from a cousin
476.s: Mr. Collins' band needed a banjo player, so he tuned it like a ukulele and played chords; a cousin showed him a piano piece.
476.q: Well, Mr. Collins, the trombone player in this band I was telling you about this while ago. I didn't want to play, but a fellow, the fellow with the head played with him died, a young fellow, he died. So, he needed a banjo player and I couldn't, didn't even know how to tune the banjo to tell the…

476.t: First music: family singing, drums, ukulele, then the banjo
476.s: Singing ran in the family; he beat drums after watching John Benoit, then took up ukulele until a band made him get a banjo.
476.q: Well, the singing, it just came natural in the family because all of us sing. Mm-hmm. That was the first. And my first remembrance was playing drums. Oh really? As a real youngster then. Who inspired you? I mean, look, who you saw playing drums that made you want to play drums? John Benoit. John…

574.t: Joe Gabriel's band personnel; learning guitar by ear
574.s: Members of the Gabriel band including Henry James; Robinson picked up guitar without a teacher.
574.q: Yeah. Joe Gabriel, he was the violin player. And Nettie James, that was the guitar player. The fellow that played bass, he called him bourgeois.

574.t: Travel by truck and train; starting in music about 1914
574.s: They travelled by motor truck and train; he began playing guitar around 1914 and in the band around 1914-16.
574.q: I used to play guitar, you know, all around. Yeah. That was before that, but around 1914 or 16, I started playing in the band.

988.t: Mike Tapplinger and the seven-string guitar
988.s: A camp friend who studied with Barry Galbraith leads to John playing seven-string; later two-seven-string duets with Bucky.
988.ch: Duo with Bucky and the seven-string
988.q: It was fun. I think, and then I started to play, I met a kid at this day camp I was working at. Because the only other job I ever had was a day camp counselor. And I like working with kids and I had a lot of fun doing it. And I had been there as a camper and I just stayed there and made a little…

988.s: Singing along to his sisters' Beatles records, then banjo lessons arranged by his father, and Pete Domenick.
988.q: Oh yeah. I think the sound of The Beatles was in our house from when I was born. I was born April 6, 1960, so when I was about four my sisters had all those Beatle records. That stuff, that sound. And I remember — clearly remember — singing along with those records at a very young age. And I…

120.t: Monk Mollencup's pianist teaches him banjo chords
120.s: A band pianist, annoyed by his wrong chords, draws him a map of the banjo and teaches him chords; Davison feels the banjo gives him no way to express himself.
120.q: Oh, yes. I always had a good ear for memorizing the lead to a song. The melody as it were. And, so, uh, all I did was strive to improve and I remember once -- this is running ahead of myself here, but-- once, being with a band and the piano player was very good; the band was a home town band called…

120.t: Harmonizing as a kid, the mandolin, and the first banjo
120.s: He harmonizes with boyhood friends in Defiance, learns scales on Butch Henline's mandolin, chords from Philip Sherman, then gets a banjo and plays square dances.
120.q: And, I immediately wanted to pick it up and play it. Of course, which I couldn't do, but I first found out that I had anything musical involved - there was a bunch of kids, we used to go down along the river where I was born and, uh, ---

92.t: From ukulele and banjo to guitar; no teachers; hearing counterpoint in church
92.s: He started on his sister's ukulele, moved to banjo and guitar, had no teacher available, and developed his own voicings, helped by hearing counterpoint at his mother's choir rehearsals.
92.q: No, I started on banjo -- I started on the ukulele. I'm getting ahead of my story. Actually, how I started playing a string instrument. My mother gave my sister, who also was a very fine pianist herself, marvelous pianist, she gave her a ukulele. And I took it and played it. My sister never could…

92.t: Teaching himself guitar after hearing Eddie Lang
92.s: Hearing Eddie Lang made him decide to be a guitarist; he taught himself unorthodox voicings over years.
92.q: know. These were real stars. So I had just been engulfed in music, just surrounded by music all my life. Now, how I started playing guitar. I heard Eddie think I had Eddy Lang, and I made up my mind I was going to play, be a guitarist. And I really taught myself, because I would hear certain…

385.t: Teaching himself guitar: tipple, ukulele diagrams, pawn-shop four strings
385.s: He learns guitar alone, locks himself in a room, buys a four-string guitar for five dollars, and gets an electric banjo through Eddie Bell.
385.q: As far as the guitar it was a lucky incident that I learned it. Cause hanging out with fellas that had a group when they had guitars-- tipple. You know what a tipple is?--Ten string guitar.

385.t: Outstanding engagements and his unorthodox fingering
385.s: The Whiteman date was outstanding; he learned guitar alone and with wrong fingering, never using the little finger except for chords.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: The Paul Whiteman thing was outstanding. The whole thing was outstanding. I had no time to time to enjoy, arrest or to do nothing. Even when I got home, I was just me & the guitar. But if I just had someone to show me to say "no, you could do it this way, or you could do it that way." Or any kind…

240.t: Other instruments as a kid: piano, banjo, ukulele
240.s: He fooled around on piano, was given a banjo and learned it before cornet, and played ukulele.
240.q: No, the only thing I did fool around with as a kid was piano. I fooled around with it. To be honest I never did turn out to really be a pianist. I know the Kord Foundation, I'm not much on the article. Your mother had a piano in there at home I guess. I just sort of picked it up that way a little…

246.t: Bands heard when young; the two Ambroses and the cheese-box banjo
246.s: Glass says he loved all the older bands, distinguishes two Ambroses (banjo and trombone), and describes a banjo made from a cheese box.
246.q: He played trombone and one played banjo. Ambrose made him a banjo, he had a banjo made out of one of them cheese box. He'd make his banjo. Who did he play with? Well he was playing with Johnny Predos and them. Wooden Joe. Well they just would move around.

179.t: Learning guitar by watching Willie Bontong and Chris Kelly
179.s: He learned chords by watching Willie Bontong in Chris Kelly's band, who showed him chords and let him sit in; he demonstrates on the guitar.
179.q: Well, that's how I come to learn, by watching other fellas play. There used to be a fella by the name of Willie Bontong used to play with Chris Kelly long years ago, and he was a good guitar player. And wherever they played up, I used to go stand up by the bandstand and watch him. So he told me one…

253.t: Uncle Chunk and starting on guitar then clarinet
253.s: Hall's guitar-playing uncle, and how he and his brother began on guitar before switching to the clarinet their father handed out.
253.q: No, my first instrument was guitar. I used to work with Thomas playing guitar. Oh, I see, with guitar? Yeah, then later on I started to play with the clarinet. My oldest brother was the same way, he started on guitar, then changed the clarinet, so I picked up the guitar and then I changed the…

474.t: Starting on ukulele, banjo and guitar; lessons and joining Isaiah Morgan
474.s: Born in Donaldsonville in 1910, taught piano rudiments by his mother, then ukulele; moves to New Orleans in 1925, takes banjo and guitar lessons from several teachers, then goes on the road with Isaiah Morgan and names his sidemen.
474.q: Well, I was born in Donisonville, Louisiana on December 12, 1910. And I started music at about six years old. Started on the piano, my mother started teaching me rudiments on the piano. But I didn't like the piano. And I put the piano down and I got a ukulele. And I started in the country on the…

391.t: Growing up in Queensland, discovering New Orleans style, learning banjo
391.s: Keating was born in Queensland in 1939; his father was a cornet champion. Records by Muggsy Spanier led him to New Orleans style. He took up banjo about two and a half years earlier and had ten lessons.
391.ch: Early life and the Brisbane band
391.q: My father, at one stage, won the Queensland Band Cornet Solo Championship. He was a relatively good musician, I'd say. I, at some stage of the game, when very small, can remember listening to Dixieland and having it appeal to me, not really knowing quite what it was. It was a pseudo type, I'd say.…

34.t: Learning banjo in New Orleans from the Hanley brothers
34.s: He started on ukulele then banjo with German teachers at Werlein's music store, took lessons from Dewey White, and later learned guitar in California.
34.q: banjo and just picked up the car a lot later no i started on the banjo i learned how to play the guitar right here oh yeah yeah i wasn't taking lessons for about

663.t: Getting a guitar from his brother; two-finger picking and slapping
663.s: Started around age eight or nine on his brother's guitar, learned two-finger picking, and taught himself to slap the box.
663.q: Just played, you know. Started slapping the guitar. Oh.

725.t: Guitar, family trio, taking up the banjo and joining Piron
725.s: Self-taught guitar, a family string trio, then banjo at Pete's urging; Piron was his first regular band.
725.q: I used to play guitar. You know, just by head like that. When I was a young kid. Sing and play. Just for past time. And then me and my daddy and my other brother, Henry. We used to play a little violin too. We had a little three piece band, you know. Played a lot of house poetry and things. And…

260.t: Nappy takes up trumpet and banjo on a bet; Bauduc's brother teaches him
260.s: Nappy played a little trumpet, then took up banjo on a bet with a kid named Demerrill. At about 12 or 13 he learned banjo from Ray Bauduc's brother.
260.q: Yeah, some kid was playing the trumpet on New Orleans. A kid named Demerrill. And, oh, I don't know, he used to kind of bug me a little, you know? Yeah. The thing about trumpet, I couldn't play trumpet. I said, well, in a month's time I'll play it better than you.

627.t: Williams buys his first guitar for four dollars
627.s: Asked where he was born, Williams says Zachary, and tells how a white woman sold him her son's guitar for $4 after he failed with a cheap first one.
627.ch: Williams on guitar technique and prison
627.q: This is my home in Zachary. Mm-hmm. Yes. I don't know Mr. Anderson Place. Mm-hmm. And we moved from Zachary in 28, nearby down there to Zion City. And we've been there ever since. Well, I moved over here on there. Skyward over there. Mm-hmm. But I made it up in my mind to buy me a guitar one day.…

763.t: First instrument: guitar lessons with Francisco Quinones
763.s: Martin's first instrument was guitar, taught by a Mexican bandsman who nicknamed him Chinito and wanted him to learn piano, which scared him off.
763.q: No, the guitar was my first instrument. The guitar was the very first. Yeah. I had one of the best professors, in fact. Well, that was years ago. You might remember, I don't forgot it was in what city it was, but the Queen's own band from Spain, New Mexico came down here. And he happened to be the…

273.t: Chaffe's instruments and lessons with Lawrence Marrero
273.s: Chaffe corrects the record on his start: piano, guitar, banjo, bass horn from about 1951. His only real teacher was Lawrence Marrero, who taught him jazz banjo style and a straightforward beat.
273.q: Mm-hmm. That was Malcolm Janay that they had referred to there and then got it mixed up. Now, the next thing I started playing was guitar. And then from guitar to you being lazy guitarist and then to banjo. And bass came in there about 1951. What kind of a bass? Bass horn, susaphone, tuba. Mm-hmm.

734.t: Family and first instruments: heel bass, comb, mandolin
734.s: His father was a farmer and steamboat cook; all five brothers played music. He started with a comb and heel-bass, then learned mandolin by listening to his cousin and brother.
734.q: Yeah, by the push. And I had five brothers of us. We all played music. Were you the oldest? No, no. I had two older than me and two younger than me. My youngest brother is still now in California. He played saxophone and kindly. He's a wonderful musician. Yeah. And I also played saxophone.

818.t: Joining Salvaggio after the crash on banjo
818.s: He joined the group a few months after the 1929 crash when it needed a banjo or guitar player, practicing from a chord book.
818.q: No. No, I went with him after things dwindled down and all that, after that three or four months of working day and night. Then I went with my first group. Then I was approached by a friend of mine to join this first group that had been organized for about two months, the Salvatio group, because…

972.t: Cousin Auguste, teaching himself guitar, early dances
972.s: He learned guitar on his cousin Auguste's instrument, then corrected a wrong chord at a family supper at age 14-15 and was brought in to play. The same long answer lists the dances of the time and his firing for the Perez, Golden Rule and Bowling bands.
972.q: Oh, I don't know. And that's why my cousin, his name's Auguste, Auguste's name, Auguste is French, but he was playing in 28, playing bass. Was his name Pavageo? No, it was my mother's sister's son, the oldest son, yeah, Auguste's name was, you see. He used to play in 28, he used to play guitar and…

631.t: Starting on bass at age six
631.s: He began on a quarter-size bass standing on a sewing-machine box, mostly learning at home as a family thing.
631.q: Well, it was more or less a family thing. I took lessons on the piano and then when I went to Chicago, I took lessons on the bass again.

432.t: No musicians in the family; ukulele contest and first banjo
432.s: His family had no musicians; he won a ukulele contest, got a banjo with LaRocca help, and took lessons from Boyto.
432.q: No, my mother told me when I was smaller. I had uncle played, but my mother bought a piano years back for my brother and sister, and we lived on 4530 South Rousin Street, but they never did learn anything on the piano. And I never did learn, but I was determined to learn how to learn. About stuff

475.t: Starting on ukulele and banjo, Green Street
475.s: French loved music, pumped the piano, bought a ukulele at 16-17 then a banjo around 1927, practicing on his truck-driving job.
475.q: So on Green Street. Way back in. Way back on Green Street. And I can remember when I was a little kid. Well I always, I always did love music. And we had a piano. And we used to pump the piano. And we used to sing by the piano. Well after I got about, I'd say about 16 or 17 years old and I bought a…

846.t: Guitar lessons, dancing class and the boyhood string band
846.s: A failed guitar start at nine, ragtime at a neighbourhood dancing class, then a youth string band that played Carnival suppers by about 1912.
846.q: Well, of course it didn't enter into anything at all. And when the marching parades happened, funeral parades, Negro processions happened to pass, they'd always come out and look at it, and listen with enjoyment, but with a tongue-in-cheek attitude towards it. My next real introduction to music, if…

282.t: Grocery store job and learning violin, mandolin and guitar
282.s: He clerked in the one grocery store and learned violin, mandolin and guitar by ear, playing Sunday nights near an oyster factory.
282.q: Well, yes, work around, in stores. Well, when he'd go to lunch, you know, I'd hand the grocery all by myself, you see. And, well, I was a water boy at the time. And they took me off of water boy and they brought me to store. Well, stay there a while.

777.s: He took guitar lessons from Professor Andre, who taught every instrument and rehearsed the band, and quit guitar because he could not sing.
777.q: Yeah, I took lessons on guitar. Mm-hmm. But I tell you why I quit the guitar. I wanted to sing. I couldn't sing. I quit.

635.t: First instruments: cello at seven, a bass from his brother
635.s: Foster started on a cello standing on a box, then his brother bought him a string bass; no mandolin or guitar first.
635.q: My sister was very little. Well, Pops, you had it here from seven years old. Yeah, but I think it was a little before that. Because my sister was very small and we were playing manor and I couldn't even reach the cello. I'd stand on the box.

176.s: He started violin lessons in 1910, later got a banjo, and recalls early pieces.

951.t: Learning guitar at Angola; music near Tuskegee
951.s: Asked about instruments, he says he learned guitar since coming to Angola, and recalls hearing work songs and Tuskegee Institute music in Alabama.
951.q: Yes. Well, I've learned music since I've been here. But I've only finished a field and I just pick up a few chords and sing with the chords that I play behind. What instrument is that now? It's guitar. Guitar. Now, what kind of music do you remember hearing when you were a kid over there in…

54.t: Learning guitar on the steamboats; first tune Bill Bailey
54.s: As a dishwasher on steamboats he learned chords from the cook, played flat pick and mostly accompanied in band style.
54.q: I was on the river, dishwasher, on steamboats at that particular time. And there were a fellow, the cook was a mandolin player. Just a little round mandolin. And I could, had the guitar and I used to kind of just plunk along, play, you know, just for myself. And he, he says, I have a guitar. I…

84.t: Guitar, mandolin and the family trio serenading
84.s: He played guitar, mandolin and drums, and formed a trio with his brothers that serenaded at Gulf Coast hotels for good money.
84.q: Played lead on that. I played in mandolin. My brother, Jujus, was playing guitar. And my brother was playing bass, Sylvester. And we had a nice trio. We used to make a lot of money. We used to go around serenading people at the different hotels in Paris Christiane, Luxie, Gulfport. We used to go…

894.t: Making a cigar-box guitar and teaching himself
894.s: Lewis began at 10 or 11 with a homemade cigar-box guitar and learned by ear with no teacher.
894.q: Oh, I started playing music, I guess, when I was about 10 or 11 years old, I made my own guitar out of a cigar box. You know, it started, it's like you take a cigar box, cut a little hole in there, and take a little piece of wood nail on there with a tack, and take some nails and put it in the end…

298.t: Learning banjo from Nathaniel Morris and finding his own style
298.s: Studied banjo with Nathaniel Morris and David Jones, practised on his own, and says he plays his own ideas, not Charlie Parker's.
298.q: That's right. I could walk back. I lived more and after we moved off to Constantinople, I lived more and general Taylor's. Right where that was right around the corner. I wasn't too far away. And what about the banjo? How did you learn the banjo? Well, I have a few ideas. I had a friend of mine,…

909.t: Buying a guitar and blues players
909.s: Morris bought a guitar for $2.75 on Rampart Street and taught himself; he did not know Rabbit.
909.q: i really wouldn't know short pants long pants well i was in long pants yeah i just used to like to see them women dancing you know when they have the blues and they'd be picking and i said guitar wasn't too much to learn no how it's just that fingering so i said i'm gonna get me and my guitar cost…

299.t: Learning guitar from his father and learning to read
299.s: The guitar was around the house; his father gave him a guitar at 11, taught him chords, and he learned to read at 14 or 15 as father worked the WPA band.
299.q: No, I was...let me see. When I learned to read I was maybe 14 or 15 years old. A little older than that. Because I didn't pick up the guitar until I was 11 years old. Yeah. So... I think I was...

967.t: Learning guitar and singing on his first jobs
967.s: King describes teaching himself guitar changes, trying to copy records, and his first songs sung on a job.
967.q: I couldn't glance the same. I learned it on the guitar. But one of the things that I did that fascinated me, since we were talking about, uh, a bird, uh, earlier, Professor Long had heard something, uh, one of his, and I can remember the words that I was doing, uh, uh, it was, uh, uh, what's the…

896.t: Banjo, guitar and learning from Dave Perkins
896.s: He played banjo in those bands and later took up guitar; his banjo teacher was Dave Perkins, a light-skinned man who taught white and black pupils and played in white parade bands.
896.q: That's right. Did you have any teachers on those other instruments? I had to teach on the banjo, but not on guitar. Who helped? My father helped me with the violin. Yes. But I had to teach it on the banjo from, uh... This man, Dave Perkins, who died.

128.s: His first instrument was guitar, bought by his sister at about fifteen; a visitor taught him chords. He later gave it up.
128.q: Did you pick it all with your fingers? No, just playing and rapping chords. Did you have a teacher or did you pick it up yourself? I picked it up myself, yeah. Do you remember where you got your instrument? Oh, my, when I got an instrument, I was around about 15 years of age.

786.s: Shade took lessons from his mother, who played guitar, and talks briefly about playing with picks.
786.q: Come over here, the table is spreading, the rocks of Asia, and so forth like that.

205.t: Bluegrass and mandolin as an early foundation
205.s: Bluegrass was the local style; Collins played mandolin as a child and sees bluegrass as improvisational.
205.q: Outside of a lot of bluegrass, a lot of real traditional, country music, bluegrass, pretty eclectic really. A lot of jazz fans, a lot of Dixieland fans and everything, but if there was one, I would say it would be bluegrass probably.

606.t: Harmonica, banjo and teaching himself guitar
606.s: Ellis played harmonica at three and banjo at seven, then outdid his older brother on a guitar using a Sears Roebuck instruction book.
606.q: Oh, let me see. Well I first played the harmonica when I was three, so I’m told, and it must be true ‘cause I can still play it a little bit, very little. And then my parents bought me a banjo when I was seven. And I learned to play that, and then somebody left a guitar at our house, and my older…

694.t: Getting a first guitar and learning chords
694.s: His brother's friend sold him a two-pound acoustic at fourteen; Perry taught him chords and he describes his bar-chord cheat.
694.q: Fourteen years old, 1976. My brother got fed up. He bought one the year before and he got fed up with my messing his scratch plate up. He’s one of those people who cares what his guitar looks like. He’s a very good guitarist himself and to sort of keep me off his guitar he prevailed on his best pal…

808.t: Taking up guitar and jazz guitar lessons
808.s: She began with folk guitar, played chords to Billie Holiday sheet music, and took a year of jazz guitar lessons in Boston.
808.q: Yeah I actually took up the folk guitar. I wanted to play like Judy Collins and Joan Baez. And I taught myself how to play those three chords and stuff. And then I guess it was when I discovered the Billie Holiday stuff I was intrigued by that and I would go buy the sheet music and play the chords…

974.t: Peabody piano, then ukulele, banjo, guitar and bass at fourteen
974.s: He corrects the banjo misquote: he studied piano at Peabody from age six and quit, then took up ukulele after Arthur Godfrey and Remo Palmieri, banjo, guitar, and bass at fourteen.
974.q: No. That’s a good, that’s a pretty good misquote. This folks, is how things get misquoted. When I get accused of studying banjo at Peabody, you can see now the trouble we have. They didn’t have a banjo major at Peabody.

338.t: Playing with Italian guitar families and switching to bass in The Strings of Romance
338.s: He contrasts his formal training with the by-ear guitar players he worked with, and how a restaurant manager's economizing moved him from violin to bass around age 18.
338.ch: Boston youth and learning the bass
338.q: Well, yeah, because I was playing with these wonderful little groups. They were marvelous guitar players, you know, like Bucky Pizzarelli here, they were those kind of players, family players that all played in the family. Everybody in their family played guitar, but mostly Italian families. And…

339.t: Hired by Bill Regis to play ukulele at the Top Hat Lounge
339.s: A bandleader spots Lewis on his porch and hires him; he solos on ukulele for a year, seven nights a week.
339.q: And so I played in the high school, you know these little concerts and things. And then one day I was sitting on my front porch playing the ukulele and a guy came by in a car and stopped in the front of the house, and says — and I wondered why is this guy out here? And he just stood there and I…

422.t: Self-taught guitar and the love of rhythm guitar
422.s: Pelote taught himself guitar from Mel Bay books and admired rhythm players like Eddie Condon, Freddie Green and Dick McDonough.
422.ch: Becoming a jazz fan and musician
422.q: Okay, when I went to college — oh I played guitar all throughout high school, pretty much on my own. I mean I am a self-taught guitar player. I didn’t take lessons. And I just listened a lot, I got the Mel Bay books for guitar and I went through the whole chord system so I could have a system. I…

750.t: Never wanting another career; teaching herself guitar at Goddard
750.s: She never planned anything but music, locked herself in a room at a Vermont camp to teach herself guitar, and describes her percussive Piedmont-style playing.
750.q: Oh, that’s a good question. No. There was no time when I thought I was going to do anything else. Well that’s not quite true. When I was, you know I guess I was probably in the seventh grade, sixth grade or seventh grade, I thought maybe I wanted to be a vet or a forest ranger. And there were all…

612.t: Brother-in-law's string band, mandolin and Joe Venuti
612.s: Williams learns guitar and mandolin from his brother-in-law, plays bass, then switches to violin after hearing Joe Venuti in Muskogee.
612.q: Well my brother-in-law was, knew quite a bit about strings and he started me out on, you know, we used to sit around the house and play old blues on guitar, and I’d watch him. And when he’d put the guitar down I’d pick it up and play blues. And he saw that I was interested, and he went and bought a…

503.t: Buying his first guitar and ruining it with paint
503.s: He saves barbershop money plus five dollars from Billy to buy a pawnshop guitar, then wrecks it with glossy paint.
503.q: Yeah, so I decided, “Well, I’m want to do something, so I’ll buy a guitar.” So I bought my first guitar at a pawnshop up on I guess it was Gratiot, near the, still at the outskirts of this area called “Black Bottom” at one of the pawnshops. And I remember it was a stellar guitar and I had written…

558.t: Bass lessons for tango and short pants at fourteen
558.s: Clarifying who taught what, he explains he learned bass to accompany his uncle's tangos and that his father kept him in short pants when he started working.
558.q: Well, the bass I learned because my uncle liked to sing tango. And he liked me to accompany him on the tangos with the bass because I could not play the accordion.

651.s: He took tenor banjo lessons from Doc Eastwood on his father's banjo and learned one tune.
651.q: No, I’m not! I know one song. [LAUGHS] “The World’s Waiting For the Sunrise.” But I took lessons on the banjo. I lugged my banjo over to downtown Louisville every week for lessons. Doc Eastwood was the teacher, and as I recall, it seemed like he really liked my tenor banjo, which was my dad’s, and…

111.t: Learning guitar from Red the bootlegger
111.s: Elvin tells how he picked up a little guitar from a man who ran a bootleg bar near his uncle's cleaners.
111.q: I just liked the sound. When I used to work a lot at my uncle’s cleaners and when I got off I used to pass a place where they sold bootleg beer and whiskey. I’d drop in to listen to Red, the guy who ran the place, play his guitar. That’s the only reason I went in

113.t: Essie Henderson, money tunes and Lee Deere's later career
113.s: In Arkansas City he learned old tunes from guitarist Essie Henderson, including 'money tunes' that gamblers tipped for; Deere later owned the Thunderbird in Las Vegas.
113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: She says, "No, you're not. I'm going to call your dad and mother right now." She got on the phone and while she was on the phone, I had my clothes and they drove up and I just left with them, before she ever got them on the phone. So I left and went to Arkansas City and I worked with a guy up there…

167.t: Taking up the guitar at seven
167.s: The house had a piano, guitar and drums; he picked up the guitar by ear and liked its sound.
167.q: And they had a guitar and I picked up the guitar and I just taught myself. Wasn't so hard for me to play it either, because I just picked it up and started playing it, from hearing the music.

380.t: Banjo Bernie's name and Callender's banjo ukulele
380.s: Callender says Bernie was the leader's last name and recalls his own brief attempt at the banjo uke.
380.q: I don't remember his name. I know he had a first name, but everybody called him Banjo Bernie, because that's what he played -- banjo and guitar. But the banjo seems to have stuck, because banjo was a popular instrument during that time. I remember when I was a youngster I used to get the magazines…

453.t: Learning guitar from a friend named Lawrence, and playing Jim Canen
453.s: At about ten he learned finger-style guitar and the blues from Lawrence, and plays a demonstration of Jim Canen with a modern ending.
453.q: It was a guitar around the house, but it was a friend of ours. His name was Lawrence. All I can remember is Lawrence, name -- I don't know his last name. But Lawrence and the first ting he taught me to play was Jim Canen, and also after he taught us the Jim Canen then he played the blues and we…

8.t: Teaching himself bass on his brother Johnny's instrument
8.s: Garland went from guitar and mandolin to bass, sneaking his brother's bass until Johnny tested him on chords and taught him the changes.
8.q: I first started with guitar. Then, I didn't care so much about the guitar. I jumped into it. My brother played mandolin, you know, and I finally picked up the mandolin and tried to play it, and it looked like I got to play the mandolin pretty fair. And I stayed on the mandolin for a while. Then I…

149.s: He tried banjo chords, gave up guitar for his fat fingers, and wanted brass.
149.q: No. I tried to play banjo. I did a few chords during that time because I didn't want to leave no instruments out. But, much as I did, I just played just a few chords. I knew quite a few on that. But, when it got to be a guitar with 6 strings, then I gave it up. I said to the thing, I said I have…

237.t: Goodwin learns ukulele, then banjo, influenced by Banjo Joe
237.s: Goodwin disliked school music, taught himself ukulele as a teenager, then took banjo lessons, first imitating Banjo Joe.
237.q: Actually in school in my primary grades, well I didn't like music. I had all kinds of things against music, you know, but a couple of times I wished I could go and hide when we had this elementary music where you had to write down a note and do all this. I'd want to go and hide. I just didn't like…

103.t: What he did before Basie, and asking banjo and tuba men for help
103.s: Jones says he tried dancing, singing and drama before drums and learned from banjo, tuba and guitar players, who told him whom to look up.
103.q: Yeh, yeh. It's just like Lionel; he took all his eggs and put them in one basket. Now you must remember the peoples that I met that I had to ask that had been traveling places that I hadn't traveled to, and they would help me. The banjo players, the tuba players, the guitar players - not the…
